title: AI log
section: Iteration 1: challenging the thresholds
text:
Iteration 1: challenging the thresholds
My prompt: “Explain your thresholds. Why did you choose them?”
First answer: skewness ≤ 0.25, kurtosis ≤ 0.5, Q-Q correlation ≥ 0.999, and 4.5%–5.5% of the means outside ±1.96 SE in total, with a short justification.
What happened next: to answer my question with evidence instead of opinion, the AI calibrated each threshold by simulation. That check exposed two problems with its own first proposal:

A Q-Q correlation of 0.999 corresponds to a skewness of about 0.17, so it silently contradicted the 0.25 skewness rule.
A two-sided tail check barely reacts to skewness: the total outside ±1.96 SE was 4.91% at skewness 0.25 and still 4.47% at skewness 1.0, because the errors on the two sides cancel.

Result: Q-Q threshold changed to 0.998, and the tail check now tests each side separately (1.75%–3.25%).

title: AI log
section: Iteration 2: “Why 1.96, and why these numbers?”
text:
Iteration 2: “Why 1.96, and why these numbers?”
My prompt: “Why is 1.96 SE the thing to aim for? And why exactly these skewness and kurtosis values?”
Answer: 1.96 is the boundary that leaves 2.5% in each tail of a normal curve, and 95% intervals are what the CLT is used for in practice. The thresholds sit between two limits: well above the Monte Carlo noise (skewness noise ≈ 0.025), and low enough that a 95% interval stays honest (table of exact tail errors for skewness 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1).
What I took from it: the cutoff is a trade-off, not a fact. Halving the skewness threshold requires four times the data. I kept 0.25 as my main standard.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 3: “Doesn’t ‘normal enough’ depend on the type of data?”
text:
Iteration 3: “Doesn’t ‘normal enough’ depend on the type of data?”
Answer and decision: the standard stays the same for every population; otherwise the populations cannot be compared and the question “is 30 universal?” has no answer. What changes is the interpretation: for discrete populations the Q-Q plot is a staircase, and for the Cauchy skewness and kurtosis do not exist, so I rely on quantiles instead.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 4: “Could we use stricter thresholds, since computers are powerful?”
text:
Iteration 4: “Could we use stricter thresholds, since computers are powerful?”
Answer: computing power improves the precision of the measurement (B, the number of simulated samples), but a stricter threshold changes the answer (n), and that cost falls on real data collection, not on the computer.
Decision (mine): increase B from 10,000 to 100,000 (measurement noise about 3 times smaller, a few seconds per population) and report every result under strict, main and lenient standards as a sensitivity analysis.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 5: questions about real data
text:
Iteration 5: questions about real data
My prompts: “There are only 141 rivers. If we take a large n, is that even real?” and “Wouldn’t it be better to measure 1,000 rivers and use a threshold of 0.1?”
What I learned: sampling with replacement treats the data as an infinite population; without replacement, at n = 141 the mean never varies (the finite-population effect). The rivers data contain only the longest rivers, and no sample size fixes a biased population. A larger n makes an interval both narrower (precision) and more honest (normality), but the threshold defines the minimum n at which the normal formula can be trusted, not the ideal n.
Effect on the project: this is why the main study samples from theoretical distributions, and why the real-data extension states its assumptions explicitly.

text:
Iteration 6: pilot runs before predicting
My prompts: “Before I predict, show me n = 1, 15 and 20 for each distribution,” then “Show the Cauchy too,” and “Run the Cauchy again with n = 100.”
Result: I made my predictions from the pilot histograms, skewness and kurtosis (Normal 1, die 15, exponential 45, binomial 100, Cauchy never). For the binomial I predicted a larger n than for the exponential because of discreteness. That turned out to be right, even though it is less skewed.

text:
Iteration 7: checking my own understanding
My prompt: “Quiz me on the material I need before we continue.”
Result: I answered the questions on n vs. B, the CLT, the standard error and Q-Q plots correctly, but missed three: the direction of skewness (I judged it by the peak instead of the tail), the meaning of kurtosis (I confused it with skewness), and how to use the formula skewness/√n to predict n. I asked follow-up questions until both were clear (the river-length histogram with mean vs. median).

title: AI log
section: Iteration 8: presentation for a non-technical audience
text:
Iteration 8: presentation for a non-technical audience
My prompt: after seeing the first version of the website: “I don’t like it. It looks too technical and has too much text. I want as little text as possible, as interactive as possible, with animation, almost like a game, so that a non-technical person can understand the Central Limit Theorem, and more colorful.”
What changed: the home page was rebuilt as six short playable levels: rolling dice into a histogram, a slider that turns averages of dice into a bell curve, an “Average Machine” with a challenge to find the smallest n that rings the bell (checked by the same four tests as the R study), a race of ten populations to the bell curve, and simulated polls. The technical report stayed as separate pages for readers who want the details.
Follow-up prompt: “The game is cool, but it feels too relaxed and playful. I want something that looks slick and professional, more like an animation than a game. Keep the game as a second option.”
What changed: a new home page (“Story mode”): a dark, scroll-driven visual essay in which about 3,000 particles re-form into each step of the argument (population, one sample, many averages, growing n with a live HUD of the R results, ten populations, the Cauchy case, and “30” crossed out). The game moved to “Play mode”.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 9: “the why-it-matters part isn’t believable”
text:
Iteration 9: “the why-it-matters part isn’t believable”
My prompt: “Make the scroll animations smooth. Also think about the ‘why it matters’ part so it really matters: what’s there now isn’t believable. And make both the game and the story not look like AI, including the text.”
What I noticed: the website opened with a news poll (“52% ± 3%”) as the reason the CLT matters, but my own results showed a 50/50 yes/no question needs very few observations, so the example argued against my point.
What changed: - A new analysis in R (Real data, Part C): how often does the usual 95% t-interval, built from one sample, contain the true mean? With 30 real flight delays it caught the truth 89.8% of the time and was too low in 9.8% of samples (promised: 2.5%). With 235 flights it caught it 94.1% of the time. County populations at n = 30: 71.7%. - The story now follows that one real example (flight delays) from the problem to the answer, and Play mode’s last level lets the reader run the same 100 studies. - Design: no purple gradients, emoji or pill badges; a newspaper-style layout with a serif typeface, notes written directly on the charts, and data sources. Text rewritten in first person with specific numbers. - Smoother scrolling: the scroll position is smoothed before it drives the animation, and the page avoids re-layout on every frame.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 10: “sometimes I scroll and nothing happens”
text:
Iteration 10: “sometimes I scroll and nothing happens”
My prompts: “The site displays very strangely.” Then: “The scroll doesn’t feel perfect. There are moments when you scroll and nothing happens. Whenever you scroll, it should be visible on the screen.”
What we found: two text cards were on screen at once, stray dots floated outside the charts, a $ sign in a table label was being read as a math formula, and the report pages still used the old purple theme. For the scroll, we wrote a small test that scrolls the story one mouse-wheel step at a time and checks whether anything on the screen changed. Before the fix, 43 of 141 steps changed nothing: several sections ran on a timer instead of the scroll, and each section’s progress finished half a screen before the section did.
What changed: every section is now driven by the scroll position (the population pile fills in, studies run one by one and then faster, a line sweeps across the “every kind of data” chart, the end of a section slides into the next one). After the change the same test found no scroll step where the screen stayed still, on a laptop and on a phone-sized screen.

section: Problems the AI found while building
text:
Problems the AI found while building
These were flagged by the AI during coding; I reviewed and accepted each fix.

Coarse-grid numbers. Before I wrote my conclusions, the strict-standard values came from a coarse grid (for the binomial, 1,000 was the edge of the grid). Refining changed the die’s strict value from 50 to about 38 and confirmed that the binomial stays normal enough up to n = 3,000.
Seed placement. The seed was first set once per grid, so adding a sample size to the grid changed the results for all other sizes. Following the assignment (“set the seed immediately before each simulation experiment”), it is now set before each n.
A crash in the refinement step when there was no gap between the last failing and first passing n; fixed.

title: Method
text: The CLT is used to justify normal-based tools: 95% confidence intervals, margins of error, z- and t-tests. All of them rest on one property of the normal curve: 2.5% of the probability lies beyond 1.96 standard errors on each side. So in this study, “approximately normal” means normal enough that these tools give nearly the right answer. That purpose drives every threshold below.

title: Method
section: Why these thresholds
text:
Why these thresholds
There is no universal cutoff, so I set each threshold between two limits:

Not stricter than the simulation can measure. Even perfectly normal data produce some nonzero skewness, kurtosis and tail error just by chance. A threshold must sit well above this noise.
Not looser than practice can tolerate. The threshold must keep the one-sided error rates of a 95% interval close to 2.5%.


Limit 1: Monte Carlo noise


Show code: measuring the noise on truly normal data
set.seed(student_id)
noise <- replicate(200, {
  m <- rnorm(B)                       # B = 100,000 values that ARE normal
  c(skew(m), kurt(m), qq_cor(m), mean(m < -1.96), mean(m > 1.96))
})
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Skewness", "Excess kurtosis", "Q-Q correlation", "Each tail rate"),
  `Typical noise (SD over 200 runs)` = c(f3(sd(noise[1, ])), f3(sd(noise[2, ])),
                                        paste0("lowest of 200 runs: ", sprintf("%.5f", min(noise[3, ]))),
                                        pct(sd(c(noise[4, ], noise[5, ])), 2)),
  `Main threshold` = c("0.25", "0.5", "0.998", "2.5% ± 0.75%"),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lrr")

Each threshold is roughly ten times the noise or more, so a truly normal sampling distribution never fails by chance. The kurtosis threshold is twice the skewness threshold because kurtosis is about twice as noisy.


Limit 2: what skewness does to a 95% interval
If the sampling distribution has skewness γ, how often does the true mean fall beyond each end of the usual ±1.96 SE interval? This can be computed exactly for gamma-shaped distributions, which have every possible skewness:


Show code: exact tail errors for a given skewness
tail_err <- function(g) {
  k <- (2 / g)^2                      # gamma shape with skewness g
  c(upper = pgamma(k + 1.96 * sqrt(k), k, lower.tail = FALSE),
    lower = pgamma(k - 1.96 * sqrt(k), k))
}
gs <- c(0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00)
te <- sapply(gs, tail_err)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Skewness = f2(gs),
  `Upper tail (should be 2.5%)` = pct(te["upper", ], 2),
  `Lower tail (should be 2.5%)` = pct(te["lower", ], 2),
  `Both tails (should be 5%)` = pct(colSums(te), 2),
  Verdict = c("nearly perfect", "**noticeable but acceptable (my main standard)**",
              "one side wrong by 2.5x", "unusable for one-sided tests"),

Two things follow:

0.25 is the compromise. At 0.1 the intervals are almost perfect, but reaching it takes about (0.25/0.1)² ≈ 6 times more data. At 0.5 one side of the interval is wrong by a factor of 2.5. Halving the threshold multiplies the required n by four, because skewness shrinks as 1/√n.
The tails must be checked separately. The total error barely moves (4.98% → 4.47%) even at skewness 1, because the two sides cancel. A two-sided tail check would pass a clearly skewed distribution. Checking each side against 1.75%–3.25% gives the same tolerance as skewness 0.25.

Kurtosis matters much less for 95% intervals: a symmetric distribution with excess kurtosis 0.5 puts about 5.2% instead of 5% outside ±1.96 SE. Kurtosis also fades quickly (as 1/n rather than 1/√n), so in practice it acts as a safety net for heavy tails.

title: Method
section: Why I do not decide with Shapiro-Wilk
text:
Why I do not decide with Shapiro-Wilk
The Shapiro-Wilk test asks whether the data are exactly normal. With 5,000 points (its maximum in R) it detects departures far too small to matter for a 95% interval:
For the exponential population, 21 sample sizes passed all four of my checks, yet Shapiro-Wilk still rejected normality (p < 0.05) at 20 of them, including n = 1,000 (p = 0.31). A test that answers “is it perfectly normal?” is the wrong tool for “is it normal enough?”, which is also the assignment’s own warning.

title: Real data
text:
Show the setup code
source("../R/clt_functions.R")

# Treat a real dataset as the population: each observation in a sample is
# drawn at random (with replacement) from the dataset.
from_data <- function(x) function(n) sample(x, n, replace = TRUE)
pop_sd    <- function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))   # SD of the whole population (divide by N)
Textbook distributions are useful because their properties are known exactly. But the reason anyone cares about the Central Limit Theorem is real data: prices, waiting times, delays, populations. This page applies the same method and the same “normal enough” standard to real datasets.
How it works. Each dataset is treated as a complete population. A “sample of size n” means picking n records at random from it, each pick independent of the others (with replacement). Then everything is the same as before: 100,000 samples per n, the four checks, and the smallest n that passes.

Figure 1: Left: the 141 rivers themselves. Right: 100,000 sample means for n = 5, 30 and 100, with the CLT normal curve.





Even at n = 30 the means are still clearly skewed (skewness 0.59). The formula skewness/√n predicts 0.58, and the simulation agrees. This was my first sign that n = 30 is not a universal answer.
Caveats I noted. (1) This dataset contains only the longest rivers, so it says nothing about rivers in general: a bigger sample cannot fix a biased population. (2) Sampling without replacement from only 141 rivers would behave differently. At n = 141 every sample would be the whole dataset and the mean would never vary. That is why the main study samples from theoretical distributions, where every draw is independent.


An election poll: where the CLT is used every day
A poll asks n = 1,000 people a yes/no question. Suppose the true support is 52%. Each answer is a 0 or 1, which is about as far from a bell curve as possible, yet the CLT says the poll result is approximately normal.


Show code
p <- 0.52; n_poll <- 1000
set.seed(student_id)
polls <- simulate_means(function(k) rbinom(k, 1, p), n_poll)
se_p  <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n_poll)
inside <- mean(abs(polls - p) <= 1.96 * se_p)
style_par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
hist(100 * polls, breaks = seq(floor(100 * min(polls)) - 0.05, ceiling(100 * max(polls)) + 0.05, by = 0.1),
     freq = FALSE, col = adjustcolor(pal$bars, 0.75), border = NA,
     xlab = "Poll result (% saying yes)", ylab = "Density", main = "")
rect(100 * (p - 1.96 * se_p), 0, 100 * (p + 1.96 * se_p), 1, col = adjustcolor(pal$zone, 0.12), border = NA)
curve(dnorm(x, 100 * p, 100 * se_p), add = TRUE, col = pal$curve, lwd = 2.2, n = 400)








Figure 2: 100,000 simulated polls of 1,000 people each. The shaded band is the familiar margin of error, 52% ± 3.1%.





A pollster runs one poll and reports “52% ± 3.10 points”. That margin comes from the CLT formula, 1.96·√(p(1−p)/n), not from repeating the poll. The simulation checks the promise: 94.7% of the simulated polls landed inside the margin, close to the promised 95%. In real life B = 1 (one poll); in a simulation we can afford B = 100,000 and see whether the formula is honest.

What the real data show

The rule of 30 fails for most real-world data. It works for the geyser, whose distribution is bimodal but nearly symmetric. It does not work for prices, delays, or populations, which are the kind of data analysts handle every day. These need roughly 51, 235 and 2,450 observations.
The skewness formula predicts the threshold well, even for messy real data: the simulated n lands near (skewness/0.25)² for the continuous datasets. One number about the population, its skewness, tells you most of what you need to know.
Discrete counts behave like the binomial. The inventions data pass the skewness check early but need extra observations because of the steps between possible values. This is the same pattern as in the binomial analysis.
Heavy tails make the CLT slow. County populations have finite variance, so the CLT does eventually apply, but only after thousands of observations. In practice that is not far from the Cauchy case. With a few giants in the data, the mean of a typical sample is dominated by whether a giant was included.

title: Real data
section: Part C. Why it matters: do real “95%” intervals catch the truth?
text:
Part C. Why it matters: do real “95%” intervals catch the truth?
Everything above judged the shape of the sample means using the true population SD. A real analyst does not know the true SD. They estimate it from the same sample and report the textbook interval x̄ ± t·s/√n. For lopsided data this goes wrong in a specific way: a small sample usually misses the rare huge values, so it underestimates both the mean and the spread, and the interval comes out too low and too narrow.
So I asked the practical question directly. For each dataset I drew 100,000 samples, built the usual 95% t-interval from each, and counted how often the interval contained the true mean.


Show code: coverage of the usual 95% t-interval
coverage <- function(x, n, reps = B, seed = student_id) {
  mu <- mean(x)
  set.seed(seed)
  res <- replicate(reps, {
    s <- sample(x, n, replace = TRUE)
    half <- qt(0.975, n - 1) * sd(s) / sqrt(n)
    c(abs(mean(s) - mu) <= half,          # interval contains the true mean
      mean(s) + half < mu)                # whole interval below the truth
  })
  c(covers = mean(res[1, ]), too_low = mean(res[2, ]), too_high = 1 - mean(res[1, ]) - mean(res[2, ]))
}

  do.call(rbind, lapply(sizes, function(n) {
    cv <- coverage(z$d$x, n)
    data.frame(key = z$d$key, dataset = z$d$short, n = n, covers = cv[["covers"]],
               too_low = cv[["too_low"]], too_high = cv[["too_high"]])
  }))
}))

What this means in practice. An analyst who estimates the average flight delay from 30 flights gets a “95%” interval that misses the true average 10.2% of the time instead of 5%. Almost all of those misses are on the same side: in 9.8% of studies the whole interval sits below the truth, four times the promised 2.5%, so the analyst reports delays as shorter than they really are. For county populations it is worse: the interval catches the truth only 71.7% of the time. With 235 flights per study, the number my shape tests required, coverage rises to 94.1%.
This is the practical cost of trusting the rule of 30 with lopsided data: confidence intervals and tests that look standard but quietly overstate how sure we are.

Limits of this extension

The dataset is treated as the whole population. Real conclusions would also depend on how the data were collected.
Independence is assumed. Real flight delays on the same day are correlated (one storm delays many flights), which would slow convergence further. The extra-credit dependent-process study is the place to examine this.
Resampling with replacement keeps the draws independent and identically distributed, matching the CLT’s assumptions.

section: 6. Why did I choose that value?
text:
6. Why did I choose that value?

Skewness was not the problem. It dropped below 0.25 at n = 30, close to the theoretical (1.19/0.25)² ≈ 23.
Discreteness was. The Q-Q correlation and the tail check passed only at n = 75 and n = 83. Near the threshold the tail rates jump as possible values of the mean cross the ±1.96 SE boundary. n = 76 already passes, but n = 82 fails again, so I do not stop there.
At n = 83 all four checks pass (skewness 0.140, Q-Q r 0.9983, tails 2.13% / 2.87%), and so does every larger n I tested, up to 2,000.
n = 30 is not enough: the skewness passes there, but the Q-Q correlation is 0.9955 and the tails are 1.44% / 2.60%.

title: Binomial (n = 5, p = 0.1)
section: 7. What surprised me?
text:
7. What surprised me?

I expected the exponential and the binomial to end up far apart, since the exponential is much more skewed (2.0 vs 1.19). Under my main standard they were actually close: 71 for the exponential and 83 for the binomial. The results table shows that they fail for different reasons. The exponential is held back by its skewness, which decreases as 2/√n. The binomial already passed the skewness check at n = 30. What held it back was the Q-Q correlation and the tail check, because its sample mean can only take values in steps of 1/n. Its Q-Q plot looks like a staircase, and the tail check passes and fails again at neighbouring n.
The bigger surprise for me was the strict standard. There the binomial needed about 900, compared with about 600 for the exponential, even though it is less skewed. My explanation is that with a narrow tail tolerance, the steps in the binomial mean matter more than its skewness. Compared to the die, each step is about 2.5 times bigger relative to the standard error (σ = 1.71 for the die vs 0.67 here), so it takes much longer to smooth out.

section: 6. Why did I choose that value?

6. Why did I choose that value?

Skewness never mattered. It was -0.009 at n = 1 and stayed near zero, because the die is symmetric.
The flat shape faded quickly. Excess kurtosis follows −1.27/n and passed my ±0.5 limit at n = 3.
The Q-Q correlation was the last check to pass, at n = 8. At small n the Q-Q plot is a staircase with an S-shape: the steps come from discreteness, and the S comes from the missing tails (a sum of a few dice can never be very far from 3.5).
At n = 8 all four checks pass: skewness -0.014, kurtosis -0.167, Q-Q r 0.9980, tails 2.44% / 2.30%. Every larger n also passes. Every tested sample size below this n fails at least one check.

section: 7. What surprised me?

7. What surprised me?

I expected the die to stay visibly discrete for a long time, since it only has six values. It passed my main standard at n = 8. What surprised me more is that it also passed the strict standard at around n = 38. Its skewness was zero from the start, so the only problems were the flat shape and the gaps between possible values. With n rolls the mean can take 5n + 1 different values, and by n = 40 the gaps are less than a tenth of a standard error. So even for a discrete distribution like a die, a larger n improves the approximation quite well.

6. Why did I choose that value?

At n = 71 all four checks pass: skewness 0.243, excess kurtosis 0.104, Q-Q correlation 0.9984, and tails of 1.83% / 3.13%. Every larger n I tested also passes.
n = 69 already passes, but n = 70 fails again, so I do not stop there. Near the threshold the skewness is sitting right at 0.25, and at B = 100,000 it is only measured to about ±0.008. My rule of taking the first n after which every tested n passes keeps one lucky simulation from deciding the answer.
Theory agrees: the skewness of the mean is 2/√n, which equals 0.25 at n = (2/0.25)² = 64.
n = 30 is not enough. At n = 30 the skewness is still 0.36, and a “95%” interval misses 3.4% of the time on the high side but only 1.4% on the low side.

section: 6. Why did I choose that answer?
text:
6. Why did I choose that answer?

Theory: the average of n independent Cauchy(0, 1) values is again exactly Cauchy(0, 1). Adding more data does not change the distribution of the mean at all, so there is no n at which it becomes normal.
Simulation: the quartiles of the sample means stayed at about −1 and +1 from n = 1 to n = 5,000 (IQR ≈ 2.00 throughout), the histograms overlap the Cauchy density at every n, and the running mean of a single long sequence never settles.
Why the CLT fails: the CLT needs a finite variance. One extreme value in a sample can outweigh all the others, so averaging does not cancel out the extremes as it does for the other populations.
Practical lesson: “the sample is large” is not enough to justify a normal approximation. For data with extremely heavy tails, a robust statistic such as the median is the better tool.

title: Cauchy (location 0, scale 1)
section: 7. What surprised me?
text:
7. What surprised me?

I predicted it would never become normal, and it did not. What I did not expect was how little changed. I asked for an extra pilot at n = 100 to see if a bigger sample would help at least slightly, but the middle half of the sample means still went from about −1 to 1, the same as for single values. At n = 5,000 it was still the same, and the skewness kept jumping between large positive and negative values. This matches the theory: the mean of n standard Cauchy values has exactly the same distribution as one value, so averaging does not help. A single extreme value can outweigh the rest of the sample.

title: Findings
text:
TipIn plain words



Textbooks say an average of 30 data points behaves like a bell curve, and the usual “95% range” depends on that. I tested the rule with 100,000 simulated studies for every sample size, on textbook data and real data. The answer depends on the data: balanced data need fewer than 10 values, lopsided data like prices or delays need 50 to 2,450, and some data never get there. In practice, a 95% range built from 30 real flight delays caught the true average only 89.8% of the time. New to the topic? Start with the visual story.

title: Findings
section: Executive summary
text:
Executive summary
I used Monte Carlo simulation in R (100,000 simulated samples for every sample size, seed 9426) to find the smallest sample size n at which the sample mean is “normal enough” for five assigned populations, and then for five real datasets. “Normal enough” means passing four calibrated checks (skewness, excess kurtosis, Q-Q straightness, and the two tails of a 95% interval) and continuing to pass at every larger n.

There is no universal n. The answer ranged from n = 1 (normal population) to n = 83 (rare-event binomial), and no n at all for the Cauchy.
n = 30 is not a safe rule. It is more than enough for symmetric populations, but too small for the skewed exponential (n = 71) and binomial, and for 4 of 5 real datasets.
Skewness predicts the answer. Because the skewness of the mean shrinks as skewness/√n, the threshold is about n ≈ (skewness / 0.25)². This predicted 64 for the exponential (simulated: 71) and came close for the continuous real datasets.
Discreteness adds a separate delay. The binomial passed the skewness check by n = 30 but needed n = 83 before its stair-step Q-Q plot and jumping tail rates settled.
Infinite variance breaks the theorem. For the Cauchy, the mean of 5,000 values has exactly the same spread as a single value. Large n does not help at all.
The standard error formula σ/√n held at every n for every population with finite variance, even where the shape was still far from normal. The shape is the slow part, not the spread.

title: Findings
section: Answers to the research questions
text:
Answers to the research questions

Sample size: is there evidence for a universal rule such as n = 30?
No. The required n depends on the population and spans more than three orders of magnitude, and for one population it does not exist. n = 30 happens to correspond roughly to my lenient standard: under that standard every finite-variance population I tested passes by about n = 20 or less, except the heavy-tailed real datasets. Under my main standard, which keeps each tail of a 95% interval within 0.75 points of 2.5%, 30 is too small for every strongly skewed population. So the rule of thumb is only safe if you accept one-sided error rates that can be off by a factor of 1.5 to 2.5.


Population shape: which converged fastest, which slowest, and why?

Fastest: the normal (n = 1, already normal), then the die (n = 8) and the Old Faithful waiting times (n = 6). All are symmetric or nearly so, so their skewness is zero or small from the start, and mainly kurtosis and discreteness have to fade.
Slowest (finite variance): the binomial (n = 83) and exponential (n = 71) among the assigned populations; county populations (n = 2,450) among the real data. The exponential is held back by skewness, the binomial by discreteness, and the county data by a few extreme values (skewness 12).
Never: the Cauchy.

The main driver is the population’s skewness, because the skewness of the mean decreases only as 1/√n: halving the remaining skewness requires four times as much data. Kurtosis decreases as 1/n and was never the limiting factor for finite-variance populations.


Assumptions: what happened when they were violated?

Infinite variance (Cauchy): the CLT does not apply at all. The interquartile range of the sample mean stayed at 2.0 from n = 1 to n = 5,000, and skewness and kurtosis estimates jumped randomly because the true values do not exist. The sample median does converge, so the right response to such data is a robust statistic.
Dependent observations and non-identically distributed observations were offered as extra-credit extensions and are not part of this submission. The real-data page notes where independence is likely to fail in practice (flight delays on the same day are correlated).

title: Findings
section: Limitations
text:
Limitations

“Normal enough” is a judgment call. I report three standards so readers can apply their own.
Near a threshold, Monte Carlo noise can flip a single n. The “keeps passing for every larger n” rule and B = 100,000 reduce but cannot remove this; answers should be read as ±5%.
The strict and lenient answers use a coarser grid than the main answer, so they are approximate.
The real datasets are treated as complete populations and sampled with replacement.
